newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Mothers to sue 'Dirty War' papal nuncio.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Mothers to sue 'Dirty War' papal nuncio.

text.p: Argentine human rights group Mothers of Plaza de Mayo said on Tuesday they will go to the Italian courts to accuse former Papal Nuncio Pio Laghi of being an accomplice of Argentina's 1976-83 military regime.

"On May 20 we will file charges against former nuncio Pio Laghi for his direct participation in the illegal repression in Argentina," Mothers' leader Hebe de Bonafini told Reuters. "We'll do this together with Italian lawyers and human rights groups."

Monsignor Laghi, Vatican envoy to Argentina in the 1970s, has been reported to have been on the original list of 1,351 people linked with the illegal repression of the "Dirty War" drawn up after investigations by the National Commission on the Disappearance of People (CONADEP).
But the Catholic nuncio's name never appeared on the final CONADEP list published in the book "Never More," which details the grisly crimes of the brutal campaign against leftists.

Lawyer and human rights campaigner Emilio Mignone said in a book published in 1986 he had evidence the original list was not published by the CONADEP after its members discussed the matter of the papal nuncio with then President Raul Alfonsin.

Laghi was Vatican envoy in the government of Gen. Jorge Rafael Videla, who was convicted of human rights crimes after the return of democracy in 1983 but was freed like all his accomplices by President Carlos Menem's amnesty in 1989.

The cleric is recorded as having said two months after the coup that put Videla in power in 1976: "There is a rare and encouraging similarity between what General Videla says on achieving peace and the desire of the Holy Father for Argentina to live in peace."
He went on to say the Catholic Church "accompanies" the armed forces "not only with prayer but with action in defence and promotion of of human rights and the fatherland."

But Laghi has been defended by the journalist Jacobo Timerman, former head of La Opinion newspaper and himself a survivor of abduction in the Dirty War. Timerman acknowledged the nuncio was polemic, but said "the history of those terrible years has a bright page reserved for him."
